fault_lines.title: 'A human reviewed it' stops being enough
fault_lines.vector: Signing a line that says 'a human reviewed it' is no longer enough. Courts and bars increasingly expect a documented verification process: a record of what was checked, how, and by whom.
fault_lines.tech_driver: Multi-step agentic work no single human fully traces.
fault_lines.build_now: Logging, trace analysis, evaluation records as the compliance artifact.

fault_lines.title: Disclosure & certification standardize
fault_lines.vector: Courts first punished fake AI citations after the fact (Mata v. Avianca was the first such sanction). Now more than 300 judges require lawyers to disclose AI use up front, and that patchwork of local orders is converging toward a single certification standard.
fault_lines.tech_driver: Patchwork of standing orders collapses into a uniform certification.
fault_lines.build_now: Verification-by-default with an auditable trail, so certification is a byproduct.

fault_lines.title: Confidentiality hardens into data governance
fault_lines.vector: AI tools that learn from what you feed them, or mix data across matters, put client confidentiality at risk. Firms are being pushed to map where client data goes and get written no-training guarantees from vendors before a tool is approved.
fault_lines.tech_driver: No-training clauses become an ethical default; vendor attestations required.
fault_lines.build_now: Data-flow mapping and vendor attestation at tool onboarding.

fault_lines.title: Regulatory convergence forces one operating model
fault_lines.vector: The rules are a patchwork — the EU AI Act, Colorado, Texas, 35-plus state bars, 300-plus judges — each slightly different. The patchwork itself is the pressure: a firm working across jurisdictions needs one operating model built to the strictest standard.
fault_lines.tech_driver: Firms adopt one framework calibrated to the strictest standard.
fault_lines.build_now: The unifying operating model. This is the whole thesis.

fault_lines.title: Liability shifts partway to vendors
fault_lines.vector: Today the lawyer carries all the risk when an AI tool fails; there is no clear legal path to hold the vendor responsible. Pressure is building, through disclosure mandates and product-liability proposals, to shift some of that liability onto the toolmakers.
fault_lines.tech_driver: Pressure toward disclosure mandates and certification standards on vendors.
fault_lines.build_now: Track for a shift; document tool provenance now.

fault_lines.title: Judicial / litigation analytics gets regulated
fault_lines.vector: Tools that predict how a specific, named judge will rule cross the line from analytics into profiling. France has already criminalized it, and US regulation is likely to move in the same direction.
fault_lines.tech_driver: Judge/jury/opposing-counsel persona simulation and Monte Carlo strategy engines make specific-actor prediction cheap.
fault_lines.build_now: Strategy stress-testing with human-reviewed, explicitly-uncertain priors; never sell 'predict the judge'. Persona models are low-confidence parameters, never determinative. (France already criminalized judicial profiling; US direction is toward rules.)

evidence.title: France criminalizes judicial profiling (Justice Reform Act, Art. 33)

fault_lines.title: The billable hour cracks under AI
fault_lines.vector: AI collapses the hours a task used to take, which strains the billable-hour model and raises the question of what counts as a 'reasonable fee' when the work now takes minutes.
fault_lines.tech_driver: Fee-transparency rules; shift toward value-based billing.
fault_lines.build_now: Measure value delivered, not hours saved.
